question_text: Find the area enclosed by the curves y = x² and y = x³.

mark_split.label: Solve for the points of intersection
Identify the upper and lower curves

insider_note: Always test one point strictly between the two intersection values to decide which curve is on top — guessing from the equations alone is where students most often set the integral up backwards.

steps.label: Solve for the points of intersection
steps.margin_note: One mark. Factor out x² carefully — do not divide by it, or the root x=0 is lost.
steps.memory_tip: Factor, never divide, when one side of an equation could be zero — dividing by x² would silently throw away the root x = 0.
lines: The given curves are y = x² …(1), y = x³ …(2)
They meet where the two y values are equal:
Solving (1) and (2): x² = x³ ⇒ x³ − x² = 0
steps.why: Setting the two curve equations equal finds where they cross; factoring out x² (rather than dividing) keeps both roots visible — x = 0 and x = 1.
common_mistakes: Dividing both sides by x² and losing the root x = 0.
Solving x³ = x² as x = 1 only, missing the second intersection.

steps.label: Identify the upper and lower curves
steps.margin_note: One more mark. Test a point strictly between 0 and 1, never at an endpoint.
steps.memory_tip: At x = 1/2: x² = 1/4 and x³ = 1/8 — the larger value names the upper curve.

lines.text: The area needs to know which curve is higher.

lines: ∴ the upper boundary curve is y
= x²; the lower boundary curve is y = x³
steps.why: Testing a point strictly between the two intersections shows which curve lies above the other over the whole interval — the area is always found as upper curve minus lower curve.
common_mistakes: Assuming without testing that y = x³ is the upper curve, since x³ eventually overtakes x² for x > 1.
Testing a point with x > 1, where x³ > x² and the order reverses.
lines_compact: ∴ the upper boundary curve is y
= x²; the lower boundary curve is y = x³

steps.label: Integrate and evaluate
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Upper minus lower, always in that order.
steps.memory_tip: Area = ∫(upper − lower) dx — write the upper curve first every time.

lines.text: Area is ∫(upper − lower) dx from 0 to 1:

steps.why: Integrating the upper curve minus the lower curve over the interval and evaluating at the two limits (the lower limit x = 0 gives 0) leaves 1/3 − 1/4, a clean fraction over 12.
common_mistakes: Setting up the integral as x³ − x² (lower minus upper), which gives a negative value.
Finding the common denominator of 3 and 4 incorrectly.
